subtype: Approach: identifying the underlying concern behind the demand [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday. Kavitha asked, for the third time, if she could cook dinner. Pradeep's mother waved her off and reached for the pressure cooker. Kavitha bit back a sharp reply and stood in the doorway, annoyed and a little shut out.

Friday. From the balcony she watched Amma move the spice tins around for the second time that week. Kavitha said quietly to nobody, "She isn't saying my cooking is bad. She's saying she doesn't want to be someone the house can run without." The thought sat oddly warm in her chest.

Sunday. "Amma, will you teach me your rasam? I'll chop and you decide the tadka." Amma's hands paused, then she pulled a second stool to the counter. It was not smooth; they argued over the tamarind. But Amma was humming when Pradeep came in.

qa.q: What did Kavitha ask Amma to teach her on Sunday?
qa.a: Kavitha asked Amma to teach her rasam, offering to chop while Amma decided the tadka.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling on Tuesday when she was waved away from the cooker?
qa.a: Kavitha felt annoyed and a little shut out; she bit back a sharp reply and stood in the doorway.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha try if Amma still wanted to run the whole kitchen?
qa.a: Kavitha could ask Amma to plan the week's menu while Kavitha cooks some of it, because that answers the wish to be needed instead of only pushing back.

qa.q: How might Sunday have felt to Amma?
qa.a: Amma may have felt valued, since she was asked for her skill and given the tadka to decide, which fits the humming.

grounding: Kavitha reads Amma's insistence on cooking as a wish to be needed and finds a way to include her.
